list.listitem: Suspect multiple myeloma (MM) in patients with bone pain, especially if associated with back pain, fatigue, nerve compression, or recurrent bacterial infections. C

Patients diagnosed with MM should be evaluated for evidence of end-organ damage with CBC, Ca+, creatinine, urinary protein, total body bone imaging (whole body CT or MRI as standard of care), and MRI of spine. Gold standard imaging is with diffusion weighted whole body MRI. C
Therapy should be initiated immediately in patients with evidence of end-organ damage. A
High-dose chemotherapy (HDC) and single autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT) is the preferred therapy in patients younger than 65 years. A

Refer to European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) guidelines that recommend one of the following regimens as the preferred therapy for patients who are not candidates for ASCT: VMP, Rd, or VRd as first line therapy, and MPT or VCD as second-line therapy. See Drug Therapy section for details.A

background.definition: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a malignancy of plasma cells that leads to systemic symptoms through its effects on bones, bone marrow, and excessive proliferation of immunoglobins or their component parts.

list.listitem: MM is diagnosed in approximately 3 to 4 per 100,000 persons per year.
Median age at presentation is 70 years among northern Europeans.
Less than 2% of patients with MM are less than 40 years, 15% of patients are less than 60 years of age at diagnosis, and 15% are between the ages of 60 years and 65 years.
MM accounts for 10% of all hematologic malignancies.
Most cases of MM arise spontaneously, although some arise from patients with preexisting MGUS.
Risk of progression from MGUS to MM is about 1% per year. The level of M protein in MGUS correlates with risk of progression.
Ionizing radiation slightly increases the risk of MM.
A pathologic proliferation of plasma cells occurs.
MM cells produce excessive amounts of abnormal immunoglobins (M proteins) and/or light chains.
Proliferation of cells in the marrow leads to anemia and impaired immune function.
Destruction of bone can lead to osteoporosis, lytic lesions, and pathologic fractures.
Vaccination against varicella zoster, influenza, Streptococcus pneumonia, and Haemophilus influenza is recommended. A
Bisphosphonates do not effect survival, but decrease the incidence of vertebral fractures. They should be considered for prevention in patients with osteopenia but no lytic lesions. B

Prophylactic antibiotics are generally recommended for ASCT recipients and can be considered in patients on other treatment regimens, especially those on new proteasome inhibitor based therapies. Intravenous immunoglobin can be considered in patients with recurrent infections. B
Suspect MM in patients with bone pain, especially if associated with back pain, fatigue, spinal cord or nerve root compression, or recurrent bacterial infections. C

When clinically suspected, order a CBC; basic chemistry panel including calcium, ESR, serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP); and urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) plus skeletal imaging with whole body CT or MR preferred to plain skeletal survey. Consider a bone marrow examination in any patient in whom the clinical picture is not clear. C
Patients diagnosed with MM should be evaluated for evidence of end-organ damage with CBC, Ca+, creatinine, urinary protein, total body bone imaging, and MRI of spine. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Less than 10% plasma cells in the marrow and no systemic symptoms
Is the same as stage 1A MM
A single lesion, no systemic symptoms

list.listitem: See diagnostic criteria in .

There are 2 common staging systems used for MM. The Durie-Salmon staging system is the classic staging system. The New International Staging System is becoming more widely accepted, and has three stages: Stage I: serum beta-2 microglobulin <3.5 mg/L and serum albumin >35 g/L. Median survival is 62 months. Stage II: neither stage I nor stage III. Median survival is 44 months. Stage III: serum beta-2 microglobulin >5.5 mg/L. Median survival is 29 months. A revised version of ISS R-ISS includes further prognostic information from FISH and serum LDH to better refine stages.
Common presenting complaints of MM include bone pain (58%), especially back pain, fatigue (32%), weight loss (24%), paresthesias (5%), or fever (<1%).

MM is often diagnosed by finding incidental renal insufficiency, pathologic fracture (26%), osteoporosis (23%), lytic bone lesions (66%), anemia, hypercalcemia, or thrombocytopenia. Patients may also present with spinal cord or nerve root compression or a history of recurrent bacterial infections.
MM is sometimes diagnosed in the process of evaluating congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, amyloidosis, or an elevated ESR.
Physical examination findings may rarely include palpable liver (4%), palpable spleen (1%), and lymphadenopathy (1%).

Laboratory abnormalities include anemia (73%), renal insufficiency (48%), hypercalcemia (28%), abnormal SPEP (89%), and abnormal UPEP (97%). Therefore, initial laboratory evaluation in a patients with suspected MM should include CBC, basic chemistry panel, sed rate, SPEP, and UPEP.

Evidence of end-organ damage should be evaluated with, at a minimum, calcium, creatinine, total body bone imaging, and MRI of spine if not previously done. Beta-2-microglobulin and albumin helps with staging. If MM is likely, M chain should be looked for using immunofixation or other means.
Protein electrophoresis typical shows a narrow spike in the alpha-2, beta, or gamma regions representing the presence of an M protein.
Light chain only multiple myeloma patients are better monitored by serum free light chain analysis than by urinary electrophoresis.
Bone marrow biopsy is helpful for establishing the diagnosis as well as for prognosis. Multiple bone marrow biopsies may be needed as abnormalities may be focal.

The standard of care for skeletal imaging is whole body low dose CT. Whole body MR gives better definition but may not be so widely available. Plain skeletal survey imaging can be done if no access to CT and should include: PA radiograph of chest, AP and lateral radiographs of cervical spine, thoracic and lumbar spine humeri, femora, AP and lateral radiographs of skull, and AP radiograph of pelvis plus any symptomatic areas.
CT should be used to clarify and questionable or equivocal areas on plain radiographs Whole body MRI can provide useful information on the extent of marrow infiltration.
Radiolabeled serum amyloid P component scintigraphy (SAP) scan can be ordered to confirm the presence of AL amyloidosis in centers, where it is available.
PET scans and Technetium-99 sestamibi scans show some promise in MM, but are not standard of care at this time.
Bone scan and DEXA scans have no role in MM.
In patients suspected of having MM, first establish the diagnosis through laboratory evaluation and/or bone marrow aspirate.
Look for evidence of end-organ damage through a combination of laboratory and radiographic evaluation. See for flow sheet of radiographic evaluation.
Patients should begin therapy as soon as they become symptomatic or develop evidence of end-organ damage.
Therapy should be initiated immediately in patients with evidence of end-organ damage. Treatment of smoldering myeloma should be limited to high risk patients, outside of clinical trials.A
High dose chemotherapy (HDC) plus autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT) is the preferred therapy in patients younger than 65 years A and in patients 65 and older if free of comorbidities. C

Refer to European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) guidelines that recommend one of the following regimens as the preferred therapy for patients who are not candidates for ASCT: VMP, Rd, or VRd as first line therapy, and MPT or VCD as second-line therapy. See Drug Therapy section for details.A

Patients with lytic bone lesions should get 90 mg pamidronate IV or 4 mg zoledronic acid IV every 3 to 4 weeks for at least 2 years. Recent evidence suggests that zoledronic acid every 12 weeks is no less effective than every 4 weeks at 2 year follow-up.B

The evidence for treatment of early or "smoldering" myeloma largely comes from small trials. The largest randomized 119 patients with high-risk smoldering myeloma to treatment with lenalidomide induction + dexamethasone, followed by maintenance lenalidomide or no treatment (it was an open label trial). They were classified as high risk based on plasma-cell bone marrow infiltration of at least 10% and other factors. Three year survival was somewhat higher in the treatment group (94% vs 80%, p = 0.03, NNT = 7) but adverse or toxic events were also more common. Treatment of early or smoldering disease should be based on careful patient selection and a discussion of the benefits and harms.
Therapy should be initiated immediately in patients with evidence of end-organ damage. The most appropriate therapy for patients with relapsed MM must be made on an individual basis.

High-dose melphalan (200 mg/m2) has long been the standard medical therapy for patients younger than 65 years and normal renal function. Currently, high dose chemotherapy (HDC) plus autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT) is the preferred therapy in patients younger than 65 years. Multiple induction regimens have been used. Regimens used include those containing melphalan, prednisone, cytoxan, alkylating agents, vincasar, adriamycin, dexamethasone (VAD) regimens, and thalidomide. More recently bortezomib/dexamethasone regimens, supplemented by a third agent (doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, or thalidomide) have been recommended (see list below). Peripheral blood is the preferred source of stem cells. There is evidence that maintenance therapy with lenalidomide following transplant may increase progression free survival. Recommended induction regimens from ESMO guidelines are shown below:
VTD: bortezomib/thalidomide/dexamethasone VCD: bortezomib/cyclophosphamide/dexamethasone PAD: bortezomib/dexamethasone/doxorubicin VRD: lenalidomide/low dose dexamethasone/bortezomib
After induction, high dose chemotherapy with 200 mg/m2 melphalan followed by ASCT is performed. Maintenance therapy with lenalidomide is also recommended following ASCT.

listitem.strong: Chemotherapy for Patients Not Eligible for ASCT

list.listitem:
European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) guidelines recommend one of the following regimens as the preferred therapy for patients who are not candidates for ASCT:
VMP: bortezomib/melphalan/prednisone Rd: lenalidomide/low-dose dexamethasone VRd: lenalidomide/low-dose dexamethasone/bortezomib MPT: melphalan/prednisone/thalidomide (2nd line) VCD: bortezomib/cyclophosphamide/dexamethasone (2nd line)

In patients ineligible for ASCT a recent trial (ALCYONE) of 706 patients demonstrated improved progression free survival and overall survival if daratumumab was added to bortezomib/melphelan/prednisone

listitem.strong: Treatment of Relapsed or Refractory Disease

list.listitem: An RCT identified 117 patients with relapsed or refractory disease and randomized them to elotuzumab + pomalidomide + dexamethasone or pomalidomide + dexamethosone alone. At 9 months, median progression free survival was significantly higher in the triple therapy group (10.3 months vs 4.7 months, HR 0.54, 95% CI 0.34-0.86) with a higher overall response rate as well (53% vs 26%, p <0.05, NNT = 4). Rates of infection were similar and 3 of 60 patients in the triple therapy group had an infusion reaction.

A similar RCT of 307 patients with relapsed or refractory disease (third line or beyond) randomized between pomalidomide/dexamethasone plus or minus the anti CD38 antibody isatuximab. With similar adverse events in both arms the triple therapy arm achieved PFS of 11.5 months versus 6.5 months in the comparison group.

Another study randomized 164 patients 2:1 to isatuximab alone or isatuximab + dexamethasone. While clinician judged response rates in this open label, industry funded study were better with the addition of dexamethasone, there was no significant difference in overall survival and serious adverse events were more common with the addition of dexamethasone.
The further addition of daratumumab to dexamethasone/carfilzomib combination in the second line setting has also been shown in a large RCT (n = 466) to improve progression free survival.

Two studies evaluated the effect of belantamab mafodotin on survival in relapsed multiple myeloma. One compared belantamab mafodotin, pomalidomide, and dexamethasone with pomalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone and found a higher likelihood of progression free survival in the belantamab mafodotin group (71% vs 51%, p < .001, NNT = 5). The second compared belantamab mafodotin, bortezomib, and dexamethasone with daratumumab, bortezomib, and dexamethasone and found higher overall survival at 18 months with belantamab mafodotin (84% vs 73%, p < .001, NNT = 9).

Talquetamab and teclistamab activate T cells by targeting CD3. In a study of 94 patients with relapsed or refractory multiiple myeloma, high response rates (80%) were accompanied by high rates of grade 3 or 4 infection (64%).

Melphalan plus prednisone with thalidomide is the treatment of choice in those patients not eligible for ASCT. The most commonly used regimen is repeated every 28 days until a plateau is reached. A recent RCT suggests that continuous treatment with lenalidomide and dexamethasone may improve progression free survival compared against MPT. Thalidomide used as maintenance therapy after HDC and ASCT improved event-free survival, relapse-free survival, and overall survival when compared with placebo or placebo plus pamidronate. Lenalidomide is an analog of thalidomide and appears to be effective when added to therapy for relapsed or refractory MM. Thalidomide therapy did increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (RR = 2.56; 95% CI 1.88-3.49). A consensus conference found that "Treatment decisions for individual patients must balance potential benefits and risks carefully, as a widely agreed-on standard is not established".

In patients who are not eligible for transplant, an RCT with 454 patients found that melphalan-prednisone-lenalidomide induction followed by lenalidomide maintenance had longer progression-free survival than melphalan-prednisone-lenalidomide followed by placebo in patients 65 to 75 years.

A clinical trial randomized 722 patients to either high dose melphalan and autologous stem cell transplant and two cycles of triple therapy (lenalidomide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone) or to 5 cycles of triple therapy. Both groups then got lenalidomide maintenance. Progression free (but not overall) survival was longer in the transplant group (67.5 versus 46.2 months).

A study compared standard therapy for newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone) in 446 patients with standard therapy plus isatuximab (an anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody). At 5 years, progression free survival was higher in the isatuximab group (63% vs 45%, p < .001, NNT = 6).

In patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma addition of daratumumab to standard therapy (bortezomib, lenalidomide, and dexamethasone) resultsed in a greater likelihood of progression free survival at 48 months (84.3% vs 67.7%, p < .001, NNT = 7).

Bortezomib is an IV proteasome inhibitor that has shown some promise in MM. Neuropathy is less common with bortezomib than with thalidomide. In a study of 682 patients ineligible for HDC, bortezomib plus melphalan and prednisone was associated with better outcomes than patients on melphalan and prednisone alone (median progression free survival 24 months vs 18 months, p <0.05). The combination of bortezomib, melphalan and prednisone was recommended as an option for first-line treatment by NICE guidance.

NCCN guidelines list the following as first-line options for patients with MM who are not candidates for transplant: bortezomib + dexamethasone; lenalidomide + low dose dexamethasone; melphalan + prednisone + bortezomib; or melphalan + prednisone + lenalidomide.

A randomized trial in 402 patients who had experienced 1 to 3 previous lines of therapy found that bortezomib + selinexor + dexamethasone was associated with a longer duration of progression free survival than bortezomib + dexamethasone alone (13.9 mos vs 9.5 mos, HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53-0.93).
Daratumumab, another new agent, added to lenalidomide and dexamethasone has also been shown to increase response rate and progression free survival in an RCT.

Two categories of new drugs which have emerged recently with approvals for the treatment of relapsed and refractory myeloma are CAR-T cell therapies and bispecific antibodies. Both categories are intensive therapy with high rates of acute toxicity - in particular cytokine release syndrome.

Patients (n=165) with relapsed or refractory myeloma following at least 3 trials of therapy were given weekly SC teclistamab 1.5 mg/kg in this uncontrolled Phase 1/2 study. The response rate was 64%, with 39% having a complete response and 27% having no minimal residual disease. The median duration of response was 18 months. A similar T-cell redirecting antibody (talquetamab) had similar findings in a study of 232 patients. The drug caused cytokine release syndrome in 80% of participants.

Patients (n=419) with lenalidomide refractory MM were randomized in open label fashion to ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) or physician's choice of standard care in this phase 3 trial. After median 16 months, progression free survival at 12 months was more likely with cilta-cell (76% vs 49%). A complete response was also more likely (73% vs 22%); there was no difference in mortality. Cytokine release syndrome was common.
A similar trial with ide-cel similarly demonstrated enhanced progression free survival compared to standard of care.

A meta-analysis of 24 studies looking at interferon in MM showed both improved disease-free survival and improved overall survival of about 4 months. However, IFN-alpha has not definitively been shown to be of overall benefit to patients with MM and is expensive.
Recombinant human erythropoeitin should be considered in patients with hemoglobin below 10 g/dL.

Patients with lytic bone lesions should get 90 mg pamidronate IV or 4 mg zoledronic acid IV every 3 to 4 weeks for at least 2 years. Pamidronate may be the preferred agent because of a higher risk of jaw osteonecrosis with zoledronic acid.
Urine output of 3 L/day should be maintained in patients with renal impairment because of MM.

Radiotherapy is the first-line therapy for solitary plasmacytoma. Lesions less than 5 cm should receive a dose of 40 Gy in 20 fractions with a 2-cm margin. Lesions larger than 5 cm should get 50 Gy in 25 fractions. Patients refractory to radiotherapy may receive chemotherapy.

A systematic review of radiotherapy versus surgery trials for head and neck extramedullary plasmacytomas demonstrated less progression to multiple myeloma and improved disease free but not overall survival using radiotherapy as primary treatment.

A systematic review identified 11 studies with 3435 patients comparing single-fraction radiotherapy with multifraction radiotherapy for metastatic bone pain. There was no difference in response rates using the outcome of pain (60% and 59%, respectively). The need for retreatment was higher with single fraction radiotherapy (21% vs 7%, OR 3.4, 95% CI 2.7-4.4). Pathological fractures were also somewhat more common with single fraction radiotherapy (3% vs 1.6%, NNT = 70).

For patients with early stage disease who are largely asymptomatic, it is unclear whether there is a benefit to early vs delayed initiation of therapy. Data from 3 trials with 131 patients found no mortality differences but did find reduced evidence of disease compression and vertebral compression.
Hypercalcemia, spinal cord compression, or renal failure should prompt immediate hospitalization.

Infections and renal failure are the leading life-threatening complications; 20% of patients have a creatinine level above 2.0 mg/dL at the time of diagnosis because of light chain excretion and hypercalcemia.
An RCT of levofloxacin as a prophylactic antibiotic in newly diagnosed MM showed reduced febrile episodes and early deaths but did not show improved overall survival.

Anemia is present in two-third of MM patients at the time of diagnosis. EPO can be considered in patients with symptomatic anemia. If there is no effect in 6 to 8 weeks, then the EPO should be discontinued.
Hypercalcemia occurs in up to 30% of patients.

MRI is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice for suspected spinal cord compression. Patients with spinal cord compression should be immediately started on high-dose dexamethasone. Local radiotherapy is the treatment of choice in spinal cord compression. Spinal cord compression can also be treated with surgery or radiotherapy.

Less than 2% of MM patients present with hyperviscosity syndrome. Manifestations include mucosal bleeding, visual symptoms, and neurologic and cardiovascular symptoms. The syndrome should be treated with plasma exchange.
Peripheral neuropathy is a common complication of treatment, occuring to some extent in up to 75% of patients. Surveillance with dose adjustment if necessary is recommended by expert guidelines.
Survival from myeloma has quadrupled in the past 40 years. Median survival now exceeds 5 years and is on an improving trend. B
Bone marrow aspirate, quantification of serum and urine monoclonal protein, serum calcium, serum albumin, and serum B2-microglobulin measurements help estimate tumor burden and prognosis. C
Risk of progression from MGUS to MM is about 1% per year. The level of M protein in MGUS correlates with the risk of progression.
Median overall survival is over 5 years with conventional therapy, is better with younger age at diagnosis and is on a steadily improving trend.
Complete or near-complete response to HDT and ASCT is associated with longer event-free survival and overall survival.
Improvement of renal function with therapy is associated with improved overall survival.
Cytogenetics appear to have prognostic significance and should be performed on patients with MM.

Risk factors for poor outcome include 70 years of age or greater, and elevated hemoglobin, serum calcium creatinine, or albumin. Other risk factors include low platelet count, 50% or greater plasma cells in the bone marrow, and elevated beta-2 microglobulin.
Patients with untreated MM should be periodically evaluated with: CBC, serum and urinary MC, calcium, creatinine, and urinary protein.
Routine follow-up skeletal survey, CT, or MRI should not be done in patients with untreated MM, unless other signs of disease progression appear.
Reduced dose melphalan (100-140 mg/m2) should be used for patients 65 years or older and those with renal impairment.
Patients 65 years and older can undergo HDC and ASCT if they are free of comorbid conditions.

For patients between the ages 65 years and 75 years, the combination of melphalan, prednisone, and thalidomide has improved overall survival compared with both melphalan and prednisone alone or reduced-intensity stem cell transplant using melphalan.

cell.label: Clinically suspected myeloma. Possible spinal cord impression?
CBC, basic chemistry panel, ESR, SPEP, UPEP.
Beta-2 microglobulin, calcium, albumin, skeletal survey, MRI of spine, bone marrow biopsy, immunofixation for M chain if needed. Evidence of end-organ damage?
Younger than 65, or 65 and older without comorbidity?
HDC and single autologous stem cell transplant.
Periodic CBC, serum and urinary M chain, calcium, creatinine, urinary protein.
Urgent spinal MRI or CT; treat as appropriate.

footnotes.footnote: CBC denotes complete blood count; ESR, erythrocyte sedimentation rate; UPEP, urine protein electrophoresis; SPEP, serum protein electrophoresis.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for MM.
feature.feature_body: All 3 criteria are required for a diagnosis: Monoclonal plasma cells in the bone marrow (10% or greater and/or presence of a biopsy proven plasmacytoma). Monoclonal protein present in the serum and/or urine. Myeloma-related organ dysfunction (serum calcium >10.5 mg/L or upper limit of normal, serum creatinine greater than 2 mg/dL, hemoglobin <10 g/dL or 2 g less than normal, lytic bone lesions, or osteoporosis). Data from Durie BG, Kyle RA, Belch A, et al. Myeloma management guidelines: a consensus report from the Scientific Advisors of the International Myeloma Foundation. Hematol J 2003;4:379–398.
